title: Project Brief
description: Start here: openspec/config.yaml is floppy's single source of truth for what the project is and how it fits together. It declares the tech stack (Tauri 2 + Rust backend, SvelteKit + TypeScript frontend, a Go rendezvous/pairing broker, and iroh for peer-to-peer transport) and the core idea — securely moving files directly between two devices, either via a short human code-phrase or a persistent trusted-device pairing. Read this before touching code so the rest of the tour has context.

title: Backend Entry & Bootstrap
description: floppy's runtime begins in the Rust core. main.rs is a thin desktop binary that immediately delegates to floppy_lib::run, while lib.rs is the real Tauri application entry point — it constructs and wires the transport manager, the rendezvous client, and the pairing service into Tauri's managed state and registers every command the frontend can invoke. Think of lib.rs as the backend's composition root that every later step plugs into.
languageLesson: Rust/Tauri split the binary (main.rs) from a library crate (lib.rs) so the same core can be reused across desktop and mobile targets. Tauri commands are async fns run on a Tokio runtime; shared services are stored via .manage() and pulled back out with State<T> in each command handler.

title: Rendezvous & Code-Phrase Exchange
description: This is how two strangers find each other with nothing but a short phrase. The rendezvous module joins a room on the Go broker (client.rs), generates and normalizes the human-readable pairing code (code.rs), and runs a password-authenticated key exchange over that code (pake.rs) so a weak phrase bootstraps a strong shared secret without leaking it to the broker. mod.rs aggregates these pieces into the rendezvous surface that lib.rs wired up in Step 2.
languageLesson: PAKE (password-authenticated key exchange) lets both sides derive a strong session key from a low-entropy code while ensuring a passive relay learns nothing and an active attacker gets only one online guess.

title: Transport Engine (iroh)
description: Once peers agree on a secret, the actual bytes flow through the iroh-backed transport. manager.rs is the core engine: it owns an iroh endpoint and blob store and orchestrates send/receive sessions. dest.rs computes where received files land (a timestamped, user-visible location per platform), and progress.rs samples byte counts to report percentage and throughput back to the UI. Together they turn a connected peer into a streaming, resumable file transfer.

title: Device Identity & Trust
description: Trusted-device transfers rest on cryptographic identity. identity.rs (the most depended-upon backend file) gives each device a long-lived Ed25519 signing key plus an X25519 key-agreement key; trust.rs persists the set of paired devices keyed by fingerprint; and sas.rs derives the six-digit short authentication string two users compare out loud to defeat a man-in-the-middle. These primitives underpin everything in the next step.

title: Pairing Orchestration
description: Building on the identity and trust primitives from Step 5, service.rs is the central orchestrator that ties identity, the trust store, and signed handshakes into the full pairing lifecycle. offer.rs defines the signed Offer/Response/Completion messages that carry a transfer handshake, and signal.rs is the enum exchanged over the wire. This is where 'is this device allowed to send to me, and is it really who it claims?' gets answered.

title: The Go Rendezvous Broker
description: The broker is a separate, stateless Go service whose only job is to introduce peers — it never sees plaintext file data. main.go wires up two servers plus a health check: mailbox.go pairs two clients by room id for code-phrase mode, buffering early messages until the second peer arrives, while fproute.go authenticates trusted devices by identity fingerprint and routes signaling between them. This is the server-side counterpart to Step 3's rendezvous client.
languageLesson: Go handles each WebSocket connection in its own goroutine and coordinates room pairing through channels and mutex-guarded maps — cheap concurrency that lets one small process relay many independent transfers at once.

title: The Typed IPC Bridge
description: Now cross the process boundary into the frontend. bindings.ts is auto-generated by tauri-specta and mirrors the entire Rust command-and-event surface as fully typed TypeScript, so the frontend can never call a backend command with the wrong shape. index.ts wraps those raw bindings with runtime shims into the ergonomic IPC facade the Svelte layer actually imports. This generated contract is what keeps the Rust and TypeScript halves of floppy in lockstep.
languageLesson: tauri-specta generates TypeScript types from Rust definitions at build time, giving you end-to-end type safety across the IPC boundary without hand-written glue — rename a Rust command and the frontend fails to compile.

title: Frontend State Stores
description: The frontend's brains are two reactive stores. transfer-app.svelte.ts orchestrates send and receive sessions — queuing files, holding the share phrase, and tracking live status — while pairing-app.svelte.ts manages the trusted-device lifecycle: this device's identity and name, discovered devices, and pairing confirmations. Both call the IPC bridge from Step 8 and expose reactive state the routes and panels render.
languageLesson: Svelte 5 runes ($state, $derived) make plain class fields reactive. Exporting a single instance of a `.svelte.ts` class creates a shared, framework-native store — no external state library needed, and any component that reads it re-renders automatically.

title: Routes & Responsive Shell
description: Steps 8-9's state gets rendered by SvelteKit routes. +layout.svelte wires the one responsive app shell — header, sidebar-on-desktop / drawer-on-mobile, edge-swipe — around every page; +page.svelte is the home transfer surface with send/receive tabs and a mode switcher; and devices/+page.svelte is the trusted-device home where you rename this device, show a code, and manage pairings. One shell tree adapts across desktop and mobile rather than forking per platform.

title: Transfer UI Panels
description: Zooming into the home route, the send and receive experiences are self-contained panels. ModeSwitcher.svelte toggles between them; SendPanel.svelte manages target selection (a shared code or a trusted device) and drives the send flow through its states; ReceivePanel.svelte maps each receive status (idle, connecting, transferring, complete) to the right screen. These panels consume the transfer store from Step 9 and visualize the transport progress from Step 4.

title: Packaging & Mobile Scaffolding
description: How floppy becomes a shippable app on four platforms. tauri.conf.json defines the app identifier, dev/build commands, and window and security settings that bundle the SvelteKit SPA with the Rust core; Cargo.toml declares the backend crate's dependencies (iroh, Tokio, crypto) and build profile; and the Android build.gradle.kts configures SDK levels and the Gradle module Tauri generates for the mobile target. This is the infrastructure that carries everything above onto real devices.

title: The Specs (Brief Closers)
description: Close the loop where you opened it — with OpenSpec. These living capability specs are the authoritative description of intended behavior that the code implements: the Tauri app shell, trusted device pairing, human code-phrase sharing, and the Go rendezvous broker. When code and intent disagree, or before proposing a change, these specs — not the source — are the reference. They tie every earlier step back to the project brief from Step 1.
